articles.title: Europe to send a diplomat team to Ukraine talks as leaders push for a voice
articles.summary: European Council President Antonio Costa said the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation EU bloc and five members of the "Coalition of the Willing" that backs Ukraine: the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
articles.body: DUBLIN (AP) — Europe will send a team of diplomats from the European Union and five individual countries to the next round of Ukraine talks, a top EU official said Friday after a summit focused on how to avoid being shut out of U.S.-led negotiations on ending the nearly five-year war. European Council President Antonio Costa said the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation EU bloc and five members of the "Coalition of the Willing" that backs Ukraine: the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Poland. "We need to integrate all of us. And for this it's essential to have a team and to speak with only one voice," Costa said. European leaders have been concerned that a U.S.-backed process will leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent. Ukraine is eager for support from its European allies. It's reluctant to leave the talks solely in the hands of a U.S. administration that has often seemed to lean toward Moscow's views. Russia does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. European leaders also distrust U.S. President Donald Trump to negotiate on their behalf after a series of tense standoffs over trade, Greenland and conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. "Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine," French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin. "There is no more U.S. support." "At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans," he said. European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement that weakens not just Ukraine but broader European security. Putin has demanded NATO troops be pulled back from Russia's borders and that no European forces be deployed in Ukraine. As envoys from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv met this week in Abu Dhabi, several European countries, including the U.K., France and Germany, attended discussions nearby, but not the main talks. U.S. envoy Jared Kushner and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after they met in Dublin late Thursday that Europe would be part of the next round of talks. Zelenskyy said Europe would send a negotiating team, adding, "They will have a voice." "We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table," Kushner said. He said Putin "is willing to give it a try." European leaders are united in wanting a place at the table. But they have tussled over whether Europe should be represented by one person — as Russia has demanded and the U.S. suggested it would prefer — or a team. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that "the Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar" and they should name a representative. Supporters of a single envoy, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argued that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy. "There are too many different groupings discussing the issue," she said. The question of who represents Europe is an old one. Europe itself is loosely defined. Is it the 27-nation EU, the 32-nation NATO military alliance made up mostly of European countries, the 29-nation Schengen zone, or the 47-nation European Political Community? After this week's U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in the United Arab Emirates, Kushner said that "if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation." That echoes the famous question often misattributed to former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger: "Who do I call if I want to call Europe?" The decision to send a team, rather than an individual, allows for participation by members of the "coalition of the willing," a group of nations that have pledged to underpin a future ceasefire with military support. That includes the U.K., which left the EU in 2020. Poland is a voice for nations on the EU's eastern flank that face constant hybrid threats from Russia, including influence campaigns and disruptive drones. It was not immediately clear who would represent the EU's institutions. Speculation had centered on Costa and the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas. Earlier this year, Costa faced criticism within the EU after his office set up a hush-hush back-channel with Moscow. Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, laid claim to the envoy role Friday, saying, "I'm the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy." "I know that the Russians don't want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?" she said. "We can't send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending." "In my opinion, calling them negotiations is an exaggeration," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Thursday. "We will not build a new security architecture simply because the Russian president, or someone in the United States, wishes it." With Trump due to head to Beijing next week to meet Putin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said European leaders feared another "Anchorage moment," a reference to the Alaska summit where they were stunned by Trump's overtures to the Russian leader in the absence of Ukrainian or European envoys. "Please, no surprises," Merz said. "Continue to play in team Europe and in the team with Ukraine." Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs noted that Europe is larger than Russia in population, economy and military might. Associated Press writers Geir Moulson in Berlin, Lorne Cook in Brussels and Colleen Barry in Milan contributed to this report.

articles.title: Dollars Rain From Balcony As Kazakhstan's State Giants Rocked By Corruption Arrests
articles.summary: Days after security services detained the heads of Samruk-Kazyna and state railway KTZ, which control 40 percent of Kazakhstan’s economy, President Toqaev convened an urgent Security Council meeting to reinforce his “Law and Order” drive, address transport governance, and reassure foreign investors.
articles.body: Bundles of greenbacks tumbled from a balcony in an upscale residential complex in the Kazakh capital as two titans of the country's economy were shaken by the arrests of their bosses on corruption charges. The following day, Kazakh President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev called an extraordinary meeting of his Security Council and declared corruption to be the "Achilles heel" of state-owned companies. The events of November 12-13 have made for a busy news cycle in Kazakhstan, even if the details remain murky. There's no clear link between the dollar downpour and the arrests, but more on that later. The people arrested on November 12 are major figures leading two of Kazakhstan's most powerful state-owned institutions. Nurlan Zhakupov is chairman of Samruk-Kazyna, the country's sovereign wealth fund. In its 2021 annual report , the state-owned fund said it controlled "almost all strategic assets" of Kazakhstan's corporate sector, representing nearly 40 percent of GDP. Its total assets reached approximately $87.5 billion at the end of 2025. Yelzhas Otynshiyev is head of Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the state-run rail operator, which has been preparing for an IPO of up to 20 percent of its shares on the London, Hong Kong, and Kazakh stock exchanges, with a potential valuation of up to $5 billion, according to a Samruk-Kazyna press release . Both men were appointed to senior roles during Toqaev's presidency after successful careers in major Western companies. Toqaev described the arrests as "an extremely serious signal of widespread corruption in state-owned companies" and said they should be seen as part of a broader effort to ensure equality before the law following constitutional changes he rammed through earlier this year. Critics have said the changes are more about cementing his grip on power than anything else. They were followed by an election in August , roundly criticized by international observers, in which a new political party dedicated to pushing Toqaev's political agenda won 70 percent of the vote. Speaking on November 13, Toqaev focused on hard-hitting anti-corruption rhetoric. He cited more than 3,100 corruption offenses identified between 2023 and 2025, involving some $560 million, and insisted that no official, regardless of position or connections, should be above the law. "There will, of course, be no distinction between 'our own', 'not quite our own' and, even more so, 'outsiders'. Our constitution enshrines the principle that all citizens are equal before the law. We must uphold this requirement," he said. Founded in 2008 under then-President Nursultan Nazarbayev, Samruk-Kazyna is also central to major state-backed deals with foreign companies and international lenders. Several of its subsidiaries, including uranium producer Kazatomprom, oil giant KazMunayGas, and airline Air Astana, have already been listed on stock exchanges. KTZ's IPO was expected to fund Kazakhstan's railway modernization and expand capacity across the vast country, including along the Trans-Caspian corridor linking China and Europe. It remains unclear whether the listing will go ahead as planned. Rubio Heads To Central Asia As US Seeks Bigger Role In Region Dominated By Russia, China Financial analyst Rasul Rysmambetov told RFE/RL that some potential investors were taking news of the arrests calmly, provided the company's accounts remained reliable. "KTZ's IPO can and should be postponed, though more for financial reasons than reputational ones," Rysmambetov said. "If it turns out this was a bribe rather than money stolen directly from projects, investors will take it fairly neutrally. Those who have already invested in Kazakhstan say: 'The main thing is that the financial reports aren't fabricated.'" Toqaev said some agreements and contracts had recently been reviewed because, in his view, they had been signed erroneously. He gave no details and did not link them to the current investigation. Political analyst Dosym Satpayev says Samruk-Kazyna and much of Kazakhstan's wider quasi-public sector have long operated like a "black box." He argues that replacing executives will not fix the underlying problems. "To paraphrase the plumber from an old joke: It's not just the tap that needs fixing here -- the entire system at the fund needs to be changed!" he wrote, questioning why Samruk-Kazyna had failed to become the kind of state investment institution originally envisioned, modeled on Singapore's Temasek Holdings state-owned global investment firm. Economist Olzhas Khudaibergenov, a former economic adviser to Toqaev, sees the KTZ arrests as an opportunity to confront entrenched corruption. He described the alleged networks inside the railway operator in stark terms: "There are legends that an entire mafia operates there, capable of sabotaging orders and even derailing a passenger train so that an honest manager is dismissed in the scandal that follows." The Horrors Of Aktas Mental Hospital: Inside Kazakhstan's Secretive Asylum He questioned whether detaining three or four executives would be enough to dismantle such networks and whether anyone would be willing to take on the backlash involved in cleaning up the company. The arrests have also reignited debate over whether Samruk-Kazyna should be reformed or broken up. Toqaev has offered no specific plan but has ordered the government and oversight agencies to submit proposals by November 24 to reduce corruption and improve the performance of quasi-public-sector companies. The same day that Kazakhstan's National Security Committee (KNB) announced the arrests, footage began circulating online that appeared to show suitcases and bundles of cash scattered outside the upscale Atlant residential complex in central Astana. The video shows uniformed police officers in high-visibility vests cordoning off the area alongside plainclothes officials. The building is close to the headquarters of both KTZ and Samruk-Kazyna. Authorities have not confirmed whether the incident is connected to the arrests or whether the bank notes are authentic. Some bloggers claimed one of the detained officials lived in the building and that eight suitcases and duffel bags filled with $100 bills had been thrown from a balcony as KNB officers arrived. Local media and online commentators have speculated that the cash amounted to between $15 million and $40 million, though no official figure has been released. The KNB did not respond to an inquiry from RFE/RL about whether the incident was linked to the arrests, how much cash was involved, or what has happened to the money. articles.title: North Macedonia: Kriva Palanka seeks help over 1,000 free-roaming cows
articles.summary: More than 1,000 cows are roaming freely through Kriva Palanka in North Macedonia, damaging property and alarming residents. The mayor wants the government to declare a 30-day state of crisis.
articles.body: Recent footage shows cattle wandering through traffic, grazing in public parks and moving between houses , sometimes after dark. Local authorities in the north-eastern municipality of Kriva Palanka say the animals have caused extensive damage to farmland and municipal property , while residents fear unexpected encounters with the large livestock. Mayor Saško Mitovski has asked the government to declare a 30-day state of crisis , warning that the situation has steadily deteriorated. According to the mayor, the number of roaming cattle has risen from around 400 five years ago to more than 1,000 today . Many of the animals previously belonged to a single family , whose members were detained after allegedly obstructing an attempt by the Food and Veterinary Agency to confiscate the cattle. However, the animals were reportedly not placed in adequate shelters following the confiscation and have since continued roaming across the municipality. Residents describe the situation as frightening , saying the cattle appear unexpectedly throughout the town. Municipal officials say they lack the resources and facilities needed to manage such a large herd . Mayor Mitovski hopes a temporary state of crisis would allow local and national authorities to coordinate resources, implement daily measures and find a lasting solution to the problem .

articles.title: Five EU countries expected to announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
articles.summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to announce a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
articles.body: Five EU countries are expected to announce the creation of a migrant deportation centre in the landlocked African country Rwanda, according to diplomatic sources, part of a broader push to boost deportations and curb irregular migration. Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands said in September they were working towards a deal with a non-EU country to host "return hubs". The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc. It is understood the scheme would only apply to asylum seekers who had exhausted legal avenues to remain in the EU, unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually scrapped by the incoming Labour government in 2024 . The five EU countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights. In August, Rwanda confirmed it had begun "preliminary discussions" with several European states. Details are expected to be announced on Monday in Vienna. Diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub in the east-central African nation is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants. The EU countries reportedly expressed hope that a centre would be running in 2027. The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role. "IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms". Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo. "Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad." The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution. Unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, the agency said. articles.title: Azerbaijan intensifies its European engagement at the EPC Summit
articles.summary: Azerbaijan added additional thrust to its engagement with Europe announcing more energy to the EU, a strategic partnership with the UK, additional agreements with Ukraine, a dozen bilateral meetings with European leaders and a new meeting with Armenia to advance the historic peace process.
articles.body: Azerbaijan is set to increase and diversify its energy supplies to Europe, beyond the current 10 EU member states, president Ilham Aliyev announced on Thursday during the 9th European Political Community Summit in Dublin.Aliyev held talks with European Council President Antonio Costa during the EPC summit to discuss the long-term energy contracts “in the context of continuing successful cooperation between Azerbaijan and the European Union in gas supplies,” an Azerbaijani presidency statement said, while Costa declared that “the resumption of negotiations on a new EU-Azerbaijan agreement is good news for our citizens.” The EU-Azerbaijan Strategic Partnership in the Field of Energy was established in 2022.Commenting on the meeting, Costa emphasized the two-way benefits of the EU-Azerbaijan cooperation declaring that “this has been an important year for EU-Azerbaijan relations,” adding that “with peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia now a reality, the EU is also investing to ensure that people across the region benefit.”Aliyev said that Azerbaijan increased its gas supplies to the European Union from 8 billion cubic meters to 13 billion cubic meters, which accounts for nearly half of Azerbaijan’s exports, and that with the discovery of new fields, the South Caucasus country plans to increase gas supplies further.The cooperation is now also focusing on renewable energy, a strategic national objective for Azerbaijan, with Aliyev highlighting the agreement reached between Azerbaijan, Georgia, Turkey and Bulgaria on exporting renewable energy to the European markets.Azerbaijan’s president said that the gas pipeline stretching from Baku to Italy, passing through the territories of seven countries and supplying 10 European Union member states via interconnectors in Bulgaria, was currently operating at full capacity, and that Baku intends to continue expanding its transported volumes.Costa and Aliyev also said that the European Union’s assessment of the Nakhchivan railway project would be completed soon and that they discussed the developments of transport links and connectivity within the global Middle Corridor project connecting Asia to Europe through the South Caucasus and Central Asia towards the Black Sea, a fast-developing alternative to the Strait of Hormuz crisis for the global supply lines.Costa invited Aliyev to Brussels to continue the discussions on EU-Azerbaijan’s cooperation given the South Caucasus country’s role in Europe’s energy supply and security.Strategic partnership with the UKAzerbaijan’s president Ilham Aliyev and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed a Joint Declaration on Strategic Partnership between Azerbaijan and the United Kingdom, during the EPC Summit in Dublin.With the UK being the largest European investor in Azerbaijan’s economy, historically driven by BP's Caspian operations, the new strategic framework focuses on defence and security cooperation, expanding trade and investment, renewable energy, infrastructure as well as artificial intelligence, advanced technology and others.British officials said relations have now reached a historic milestone and both leaders committed to expanding mutual trade, defence cooperation, and private-sector investment ties under the new accord. With Russia watching on, the UK and Azerbaijan agreed to “strengthening cooperation in defence and security in support of regional peace and stability” (...) “across a broad spectrum of security priorities, in response to evolving security challenges and threats.”The two sides also agreed to “support the development of the Middle Corridor, alongside transport, logistics and infrastructure projects that facilitate cross-border trade and investment.”Securing the Ukrainian grid and drone agreementsUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a “detailed discussion” with President Aliyev during the EPC summit, focusing on emergency support for Ukraine's battered energy grid ahead of the harsh winter and post-conflict reconstruction strategies.Zelenskyy confirmed that contracts were signed under the so-called “Drone Deal,” an ongoing bilateral drone agreement, saying that “we are working to scale up orders,” adding that “relations between our countries are developing.”Zelenskyy also thanked Aliyev for Azerbaijan's humanitarian assistance as officials confirmed an ongoing €1.35 million emergency grid support package from Baku, comprising heavy electrical equipment and generators. Total Azerbaijani humanitarian aid to Ukraine has now reached €48 million, focusing on civilian energy infrastructure and medical rehabilitation. Ukraine’s president also noted that Kyiv is closely analysing Azerbaijan's post-conflict reconstruction across Karabakh and the East Zangezur regions, as the Ukrainian government views Baku's massive infrastructural overhaul as a viable blueprint for its own eventual post-war recovery.The two leaders also discussed expanding economic and trade relations, including private-sector economic cooperation, with Zelenskyy saying that “we value the fact that companies are staying and continuing to work for our people, often despite Russia’s vile attacks.”Advancing the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace processBuilding on their historic peace process, Azerbaijan’s president Ilham Aliyev held new talks with Armenian prime minister Nikol Pashinyan on advancing their peace consolidation, border delimitations, water cooperation and interconnection of electricity grids as well as more confidence-building measures.The two leaders also discussed the progress of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) connectivity project, including the planning of its railway and highway components.Since November 2025, a total of 105,000 tonnes of cargo have been transported to Armenia through the territory of Azerbaijan.Broadening European engagementPresident Aliyev met with Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis for talks on upgrading the Southern Gas Corridor's infrastructure in the context of Azerbaijani-Greek bilateral relations, anchored by the Trans Adriatic Pipeline (TAP). Aliyev also held talks with Moldovan President Maia Sandu on energy cooperation and on strengthening Moldova’s energy security as well as economic and trade ties with a particular focus on the agricultural sector.Azerbaijan’s president met his Romanian counterpart Nicusor Dan for the first time to discuss energy and connectivity projects, focusing on linking the Caspian and the Black Seas.Dan said in a post on X that “we focused on deepening our Strategic Partnership, advancing key energy and connectivity projects, and pursuing an ambitious shared political and economic agenda,” adding that “our cooperation, linking the Caspian and the Black Sea, has strong potential to grow.”Aliyev also held energy talks with Bulgaria’s prime minister Rumen Radev and Czech prime minister Andrej Babis.

articles.title: Russia sends major business delegation to Kabul for business talks with the Taliban
articles.summary: A Russian deputy prime minister led a 70-strong Russian delegation to Afghanistan, pursuing deals on transport, logistics, agriculture, and health products with the Taliban.
articles.body: Russian deputy prime minister Alexei Overchuk was welcomed by a guard of honour when he arrived in Kabul on Thursday with a delegation of 70 Russian business people to conduct business talks with the Taliban government, Afghan officials said.Overchuk met Taliban prime minister Mohammad Hassan Akhund, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs Abdul Ghani Baradar as well as foreign minister Amir Khan Muttaqi.According to a statement by the Afghan government published on X, Abdul Ghani Baradar described to the Russians Afghanistan's potential for economic development and investment, pointing to "strategic location, abundant resources and a workforce of 24 million people".Abdul Ghani Baradar invited Russian companies to invest in agriculture, mining, constructions of roads, railways and factories, and to create a special economic zone in Afghanistan, while expressing his wish to expand exports of Afghan agricultural products to Russia.The deputy prime minister also asked Russia to "provide the necessary facilities for Afghan products to be supplied to Russian markets and to cooperate in reducing transport and transit costs".A Russian news agency quoted Alexei Overchuk as saying that the Russian delegation represent companies that are already operating in Afghanistan and that "many others want to start operating in this country."Overchuk said that the companies represented in the delegation work in the fields of transport, logistics, agriculture and pharmaceuticals and that the Afghan government is interested in Russian chemical fertilisers, as well as in "building fertiliser production plants on Afghan soil".Overchuk estimated that trade between Russia and Afghanistan in the first eight months of 2026 had more than doubled, reaching over 349 million dollars.Russia officially recognised the Taliban government in July 2025, being the only state to have taken such a step since the Taliban seized power in August 2021, after the withdrawal of the United States.Although no country other than Russia has formally recognised the new Afghan regime, the Taliban authorities have so far held high-level talks with many states and have established specific diplomatic and economic relations with some governments.

articles.title: Bahrain Says It Intercepted Iranian Attacks As Tehran Claims Strike On US Base
articles.summary: Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks on November 15, after explosions and air raid sirens were reported across the Gulf kingdom and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it had targeted a US military installation.
articles.body: Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks on November 15, after explosions and air raid sirens were reported across the Gulf kingdom and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed it had targeted a US military installation. The Bahraini military said its air defenses intercepted several attacks before they reached their targets, accusing Tehran of continuing its "systematic hostile approach" toward the kingdom. Bahrain's Foreign Ministry said the country rejected "turning its territory into an arena for settling scores" and held Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences. Iran's IRGC claimed they had launched six drones targeting a US air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain, according to statements carried by Iranian state media. There was no immediate confirmation from US or Bahraini authorities that the radar installation had been hit. Citing its journalists in Bahrain, the AFP news agency reported that explosions were heard around 4 a.m. local time, followed by another series of blasts around 6:30 a.m. Sirens also sounded and Bahraini authorities issued warnings urging residents to seek shelter without specifying the source of the threat. The Interior Ministry told residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow official channels for updates. Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, has been among the Gulf countries targeted by Iran during the conflict, which began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes on Iran. The reported attack on November 15 came two days after the IRGC said it had targeted a US early-warning radar facility in Bahrain. The US military said at the time that it had intercepted two Iranian drones targeting the island, reporting no casualties or damage. Bahrain has now been targeted twice in three days, following a lull in attacks. The latest developments come amid diplomatic efforts to end the nearly nine-month conflict, which have not yet produced a breakthrough despite a broader lull in fighting. Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key global oil transit route, and launched missile and drone attacks on military and civilian infrastructure across the region. US President Donald Trump has told his senior advisers in recent days that he might refrain from further attacks on Iran if Tehran and Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen avoid new provocations, according to Reuters. Trump has also said the US naval blockade of Iran would remain in place. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's military said on November 15 it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh and three drones in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province. articles.title: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
articles.summary: The MP lost both of her legs after the alleged attack outside her electorate office four weeks ago.
articles.body: Independent MP Helen Haines has been released from hospital after an alleged attack last month Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee. The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia. Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas. In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery. "This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said. "I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing." She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour. Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife. Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established. Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns. The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate. Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family. "All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement. "We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation." 'Targeted' attack on much-loved MP leaves Australian town heartbroken

articles.title: Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics
articles.summary: The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.
articles.body: When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage. But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation. For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women , minorities and LGBTQ+ people . During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban. Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government. Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal , which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP , headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates. Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife. "If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing. Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey . Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists , opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations. Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation. In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats . In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet , were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin. In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel , then working for German newspaper Die Welt , was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara. Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups . Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala , who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison. Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu , and a number of journalists. Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years. On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges. "What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law." These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said. For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue." In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria , or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey. The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt. This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy. In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges. But Tas said that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment." articles.title: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips
articles.summary: The fallout of Jensen Huang's downfall expanded into a public fight between two of President Trump's top advisers. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia's most advanced chips.
articles.body: The fallout of Jensen Huang’s downfall expanded into a public fight between two of President Trump’s top advisers. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Nick Schifrin looks at the finger-pointing and the ongoing efforts to control advanced technology exports to China. Amna Nawaz: Today, the fallout of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's downfall expanded into a public fight between two of President Trump's top advisers. The treasury secretary accused the commerce secretary of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia's most advanced chips. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang played an outsized role in President Trump's technology policy. Nick Schifrin looks at today's finger-pointing and the ongoing efforts to control advanced technology exports to China. Jensen Huang: Here it is, our brand-new GeForce RTX 50 Series Blackwell architecture. Nick Schifrin: They're the American chips powering the AI revolution. And, for years, Jensen Huang wanted them sold to China. Woman: Jensen, how do you like China? Jensen Huang: I love China. Nick Schifrin: And Huang had an administration ally. Jensen Huang: Howard is the person I talked to most in the administration. Nick Schifrin: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose agency controls the entity list of countries and companies banned from buying U.S. technology. Howard Lutnick: We want to keep having the Chinese use the American technology stack. Nick Schifrin: Last year, Commerce and the Trump administration decided to let China buy some less advanced Nvidia chips. But international companies believed to collaborate with Beijing, including the Singapore-based Megaspeed, the company whose leader Huang had an affair with, reportedly gave China access to the most advanced chips. And, today, Lutnick was accused of looking the other way. Scott Bessent: Treasury, War, USTR, and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months. But Commerce has the pen. Nick Schifrin: Today, on CNBC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for not implementing the U.S.' export blocks on Nvidia's most advanced chips. Scott Bessent: I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s. And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the -- our -- hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage. Chris McGuire, Council on Foreign Relations: If we did prevent them from getting these chips, they actually would be, instead of months behind us in AI, they would be years behind us in AI. Nick Schifrin: Chris McGuire is a senior fellow on the council of foreign relations and was the director of technology on President Biden's National Security Council staff. He says the effort to restrict Chinese access to chips began when the first Trump administration blocked the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei from buying semiconductors with U.S. technology. The U.S. realized the export restrictions were some of the best ways to constrain Chinese military and AI advancements, so they continued into the Biden administration. And, in early 2025, the Biden team pushed through new regulations that required most foreign companies to get Commerce Department permission to buy advanced chips. Chris McGuire: It was slated to go into effect in May 2025, but two days before it went into effect, the Commerce Department said they're not enforcing it. If the Commerce Department had enforced this, Megaspeed would not have been able to get chips unless the U.S. government green-lighted it. But because they didn't enforce it, Megaspeed could just buy whatever they wanted completely uninterrupted. Nick Schifrin: Today, Bessent also blamed Nvidia for selling to Megaspeed. Scott Bessent: Did Nvidia know their client? And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? Nick Schifrin: But it was Huang, who is a celebrity in China, who helped push President Trump to allow the sale of U.S. chips to China in the first place. Jensen Huang: Why is it that we don't come up with a regulation that's more balanced so that Nvidia can win around the world, instead of giving up the world? We want United States to win at every single layer, including the chip layer. And conceding the entire market is not going to allow the United States to win the technology race long term. Chris McGuire: Well, Jensen certainly wins if they if they sell chips to China, but I would argue America does not win. Nick Schifrin: In fact, independent researchers this week discovered that China's AI models were all developed thanks to smuggled Nvidia advanced chips. Chris McGuire: While I think the poor implementation on export controls has probably cost us years of advantage, we still -- doubling down now will still give us years, even potentially decades of advantage in the future, as long as we actually manage it right. But if we don't, China is going to stay close and that will have catastrophic impacts for U.S. national security. Nick Schifrin: There's a debate over that, which will continue. But Jensen Huang's departure will empower advocates of stricter export controls, including a push on Capitol Hill to further restrict the world's leading technology from going to the U.S.' chief international competitor. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Nick Schifrin.

articles.title: Amid Ongoing Battle Over Afghan Deportations, US Legislators Push Law Granting Protection
articles.summary: US plans to deport 150 Afghans back to their homeland have sparked fears for their safety and have led to court battles. Now, US legislators are pushing a new law to stop flights taking off.
articles.body: US plans to deport 150 Afghans back to their homeland via Pakistan have sparked fears for their safety and led to a series of court hearings that have so far prevented the flight taking off. But this week, activists and lawmakers have been been promoting legislation on Capitol Hill to provide longer-term protection for thousands of Afghans across the United States. Democrats will be able to force a vote in the House of Representatives when their new majority takes control of Congress in January. But dozens of meetings have been held this week aimed at securing bipartisan support, given what its supporters see as the urgency of the situation around planned flights. “The issue is trying to get it done this term fast enough to make sure that we put some pressure on stopping these flights,” Democratic Congressman Scott Peters told RFE/RL. “We're working with Republicans we think might be supportive as well.” US authorities revoked Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for thousands of Afghans in May last year. "Afghanistan has had an improved security situation, and its stabilizing economy no longer prevents them from returning to their home country," then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem said at the time. Noem’s successor Markwayne Mullin does not appear to have commented on specifically Afghan TPS but speaking more generally about Trump administration actions to remove TPS status from 13 nations , he has stated that "TPS was temporary, it was never meant to be permanent status." "You had an opportunity while you were here to try to change your status,” Mullin told a news conference in New York on July 1. “You have to go back to a country that they'll either take you, or back to the country you came from." The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) estimated last year that there were some 11,700 Afghan nationals with TPS status. Taliban Concerned Amid Reports Of US Deportation Of Afghans Via Pakistan The new legislation, called the Afghanistan TPS Act, would restore their status. It would also make TPS available to other Afghans, including at least some of the 150 people on the planned deportation flight. The bill was drafted by Democratic Congressman Jason Crow, who served in Afghanistan with the US military. He has been taking part in the push for support in Washington this week, along with US and Afghan veterans of the 20-year US-led fight against the Taliban and Al-Qaeda that followed the 9/11 attacks on New York and Washington in 2001. “Our Afghan partners put their lives on the line to help protect American servicemembers like me," Crow said. "After more than two decades of war, we made a promise that we’d look after them. It’s both a moral and national security imperative that we keep that promise.” The deportations issue is causing grave concern among the Afghan community in the United States. Several people have told RFE/RL’s Radio Azadi that they are worried about themselves or their loved ones. “Families in our communities are afraid,” Zarif Aminyar, an Afghan-born business executive and activist, told a public meeting this week in Sacramento, California -- home to one of the country’s largest Afghan diasporas. “They’re afraid that the country they sought for safety is no longer hearing their humanity.” Multiple US media reports in early November said that US authorities were set to deport 150 Afghans through a flight from Louisiana to Pakistan and then onward to Afghanistan. A court ruling on November 3 granted a four-day temporary restraining order. A further ruling on November 7 extended this indefinitely. “The complaint more than adequately alleges that the Afghan nationals face a likelihood of irreparable harm if deported from this country and transported to Pakistan to be turned over to the Taliban,” stated Judge Victor Marrero in his November 7 ruling. US Court Temporarily Blocks Deportation Of Afghan Nationals Over Safety Concerns But this ruling only applies to five people represented by Project Rousseau, a US non-governmental organization that brought the case to court. Shawn VanDiver, a former serviceman who is head of AfghanEvac, a group campaigning on this issue, told RFE/RL that a deportation flight was planned for next week. “The flight for the 150 is rescheduled to November 16,” he said. “They all have final orders of removal.” “For operational security reasons and the safety of our officers, we would not confirm future removal operations,” a spokesman told RFE/RL. “Temporary Protected Status (TPS) is exactly that -- temporary. For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent,” he said. “What we would say now is: It’s closing time…The good news is it’s not too late to get a $3,000 check and a free flight home,” he added, referring to conditions for a voluntary deportation program. Supporters of the legislation need 218 signatures on a discharge petition to force a House vote, requiring the backing of at least four lawmakers beyond the chamber's 214 Democrats. Outgoing Congressmen Don Bacon and Brian K. Fitzpatrick are among the Republican supporters of the legislation. The act “provides temporary protection and work authorization for eligible Afghans who are already here, while requiring biometric and biographic information and criminal and national-security background checks,” stated Bacon when the bill was introduced. Midterm Democrat Gains Likely To Put Trump's Russia, Ukraine, Iran Policies Under Pressure If the vote clears the House and then the Senate, another question is whether US President Donald Trump would sign it. “You know, one step at a time, right? I mean, that'd be a good problem to have if we can get this thing passed out of Congress,” said Peters, who wrote an open letter signed by 66 Democrat lawmakers calling on Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to stop the deportation flight. “He has, even sometimes when he's not signed a bill, taken the political signal and cooperated. And any way we can stop these flights would be great.” Ray Furlong is a Senior International Correspondent for RFE/RL. He has reported for RFE/RL from the Balkans, Kazakhstan, Georgia, and elsewhere since joining the company in 2014. He previously worked for 17 years for the BBC as a foreign correspondent in Prague and Berlin, and as a roving international reporter across Europe and the former Soviet Union. RFE/RL's Radio Azadi is one of the most popular and trusted media outlets in Afghanistan. Nearly half of the country's adult audience accesses Azadi's reporting on a weekly basis.

articles.title: Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back as rebels advance
articles.summary: Forces aligned with the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia are seeking to strengthen control over the interim capital Aden as the Iran-backed Houthis approach.
articles.body: The Southern Armed Forces group allied with Yemen's UN-recognized government and backed by Saudi Arabia said Sunday they had repositioned themselves away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Southern Armed Forces said the repositioning is intended to secure the southern city of Aden, "and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the frontlines and addressing existing threats." Aden, which has a population of over a million people, is the interim seat of the Yemeni government, formally known as the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC). The Southern Armed Forces also intend to end the Houthi siege over the strategic southwestern city of Taiz. Nearly two million people live in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city. The siege is raising fears of famine for residents, as well as a possible medical crisis as hospitals face restricted supplies. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Houthis control much of northwest Yemen , including the capital Sanaa. The rebels are a Shiite militant group backed by Iran. The US, Canada and several other countries regard them as a terror organization. The Houthis in September launched a rapid offensive against the PLC, seizing much of the coastline along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. The Houthis have taken control of the major port town of Mocha in September, firming their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The latest redeployment of the Southern Armed Forces is likely to give the rebels even more control over the strategic area. Sources told AFP news agency that Houthi forces are now just 60 kilometers (less than 40 miles) from Aden. The fighting in Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, has been fueled by the wider rivalry between Iran and Saudi Arabia. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In recent weeks, the Houthis have been launching frequent attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, the rebels claimed that they targeted the King Khalid International Airport and financial district of the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the alleged Houthi attack.

articles.title: Nikoloski: respect for the Constitutional Court shows institutional maturity
articles.summary: As a Government, we are making every effort to establish a functional system of the rule of law as the foundation of a democratic state, and here, of course, one of the key actors is the Constitutional Court, which has a special and irreplaceable role in preserving the constitutional order and protecting fundamental rights and freedoms, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Aleksandar Nikoloski…
articles.body: As a Government, we are making every effort to establish a functional system of the rule of law as the foundation of a democratic state, and here, of course, one of the key actors is the Constitutional Court, which has a special and irreplaceable role in preserving the constitutional order and protecting fundamental rights and freedoms, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Aleksandar Nikoloski said in his address at the fourth annual conference of the Forum of Balkan Constitutional Courts, held in Ohrid on the topic “Contemporary Challenges to the Rule of Law: The Role of Constitutional Courts.” Nikoloski stressed that the role of the Constitutional Court is particularly important in this time of rapid social, technological, and political changes. As he put it, “that is why institutions must be stable, institutions must be resilient, and institutions must survive political changes.” The independence, professionalism, and integrity of constitutional judges and of the Constitutional Court are key to fulfilling this function. The rule of law implies not only the adoption of high-quality decisions, but also their respect and implementation. The executive and legislative branches have the responsibility to create the conditions for the full implementation of the decisions of the Constitutional Court, which very often also mean a correction of certain decisions that may have been taken without sufficient analysis and without sufficiently taking all the facts into account, and sometimes even with some other intention. That is why the foundation of the Constitutional Court is precisely this — to help make corrections where corrections need to be made, Nikoloski pointed out. He noted that respect for constitutional justice is an indicator of a state’s institutional maturity and democratic responsibility. That is why we strive to respect the Constitutional Court and to give it the place it deserves in the state-legal order. The independence of the judiciary should, of course, not be understood in isolation from the other institutions, but rather as a guarantee of impartial and objective decision-making, and also as a way of improving society. Mutual control and balance among the three branches of power — and here, of course, the Constitutional Court as a separate body — play a significant role in maintaining a functional state, Nikoloski emphasized in his address before constitutional judges from the country and abroad. The Deputy Prime Minister also referred to the new challenges, such as digitalization and artificial intelligence, which on the one hand can be an advantage, but on the other hand also a threat. Of course, knowledge, experience, and the human factor remain irreplaceable, and I cannot agree with certain debates that are being conducted, that even in this area — in the area of respecting the Constitution, in the area of implementing the Constitution, and in the area of implementing and respecting the laws — we should rely on artificial intelligence. I think that is wrong, and I think it is something that we need to think about very seriously as a state and as states, because this is a broader debate, not only in our country, but I repeat, I believe that is not the path we should follow, because knowledge and personal experience are something that is irreplaceable and that no machine can do, Nikoloski said. At the closing of the Forum of Balkan Constitutional Courts, Deputy Prime Minister Nikoloski stressed that a strong state does not mean only a strong executive power, but a limited executive power, a state with strong and independent institutions, institutions that complement each other and control one another. Therefore, as a representative of the executive branch, as Deputy Prime Minister, I can say that as a Government we will do everything and we are doing everything for this system to continue to function and to be further developed, Nikoloski said.

articles.title: Appeals Court Lifts House Arrest on Klevi Metaj, Student Symbol of Albania’s Protests, as Police Keep Issuing On-the-Spot Fines
articles.summary: Tirana’s Court of Appeals on Friday lifted the house arrest imposed on Klevi Metaj, the 22-year-old law student who became the face of Albania’s student protests after footage showed him clashing with police officers and later handcuffed to the railings of the Ministry of Education.
articles.body: Tirana’s Court of Appeals on Friday lifted the house arrest imposed on Klevi Metaj, the 22-year-old law student who became the face of Albania’s student protests after footage showed him clashing with police officers and later handcuffed to the railings of the Ministry of Education. The court replaced house arrest with an obligation to report once a month to the relevant authority, according to Metaj’s lawyers. They had appealed the earlier decision of the Tirana court of first instance, which ordered house arrest after he was detained at the Oct. 13 protest . The lawyers said a criminal complaint has also been registered against the police officers involved, over what they describe as degrading and inhuman treatment of Metaj during his detention. Metaj, a University of Tirana student, became widely known on Oct. 13, when students clashed with police outside the Education Ministry. Photos showed him handcuffed to the ministry’s fence, and other images showed him with visible injuries inside a police van. He was taken to a hospital, where he was handcuffed to his bed. The Tirana court then ordered house arrest. On Friday, the Court of Appeals lifted that measure. The ruling comes as police continue to fine protesters on the spot under two emergency acts the government adopted in late October . Since the acts took effect, police have fined protesters 5,000 lek (about €55 or $62) each, mainly for blocking roads or standing peacefully on the boulevard. Partial police figures show more than 65 people fined. Media outlets and civil society groups count more than 100 , and they say the real number is likely higher because not all fines are reported. Unlike Metaj, those fined have not been brought before a judge. Lawyers and rights groups say the fines are imposed at the scene, without a court review or an individual assessment of what each person did. The government’s package also includes measures that give police the right to restrict protests near institutions, remove people from designated “protected zones” and fine participants. Fines can reach 500,000 lek (about €5,500 or $6,200). Last week, student groups asked the Constitutional Court to strike down the acts and to suspend them until it rules on their constitutionality. The protests began on May 31 over a tourism project in the protected Zvernec area on the southern coast. They grew into a broader movement against corruption and the rising cost of living, and in October students clashed with police in Tirana. Protesters are demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

articles.title: Moscow Designates Deputy FM Galuzin as Zurabashvili’s Counterpart in Russia-Georgia Talks
articles.summary: Russia has designated Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin as its counterpart to Georgia’s newly appointed special representative for relations with Russia, George Zurabashvili, and has established contact with the Georgian official, the Russian Foreign Ministry told the Russian newspaper Izvestia.
articles.body: Russia has designated Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin as its counterpart to Georgia’s newly appointed special representative for relations with Russia, George Zurabashvili, and has established contact with the Georgian official, the Russian Foreign Ministry told the Russian newspaper Izvestia. “The appointment of Georgia’s First Deputy Foreign Minister George Zurabashvili as the Prime Minister’s special representative for relations with Russia reflects Tbilisi’s interest in maintaining and developing channels of communication with our country," Izvestia cited the Russian MFA as saying. "We welcome this. Russia has consistently advocated for building pragmatic and mutually beneficial relations with Georgia. We have established contact with George Zurabashvili," the Ministry added. 11/08/2026 - Russia’s Galuzin Reiterates Openness to ‘Further Expanding Pragmatic Ties’ with Tbilisi Zurabashvili, Georgia’s First Deputy Foreign Minister, was appointed as the Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze's Special Representative for Relations with Russia on October 21, filling a position that had remained vacant since December 2025. He was allowed to retain his current position at the Foreign Ministry, a decision that also required Georgia's parliament to adopt the respective legislative changes in October. The appointment has drawn concern among former Georgian diplomats, who warned of a “dangerous trend” and questioned whether the move could amount to de facto restoring diplomatic relations with Moscow. Kobakhidze's remarks while presenting the new Special Representative also left an impression among professional circles that Tbilisi was expanding the post’s mandate, previously limited to trade, economic, humanitarian, and cultural issues, to now also cover “the peaceful resolution of the conflict with the Russian Federation." The post of a Special Representative was established as part of the informal direct dialogue between Georgia and Russia launched in late 2012, commonly known as the Abashidze-Karasin format. Grigory Karasin, Russia's initial representative, also served as Russian Deputy Foreign Minister from 2005 to 2019. The Russian Foreign Ministry described the move as involving "the resumption of the Russian-Georgian dialogue, which was launched in 2012 and operated for nearly 10 years," considering "this mechanism, known as the 'Karasin-Abashidze format,' to be successful and useful." 02/02/2023 - Karasin-Abashidze Audio Recording Sparks Opposition Criticism Izvestia further cited the Russian MFA as saying that it views "the promotion of people-to-people contacts, the development of trade and economic cooperation, tourism, transportation links, and the implementation of cultural projects as the priority tasks of this new channel of communication." It also expressed hope that "Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s decision to appoint a special representative for relations with Russia will give the Russian-Georgian dialogue additional momentum and allow us to place bilateral cooperation on a more systematic basis." Zurabashvili replaced Giorgi Kajaia, who took up the post in March 2024 after a four-year term as Head of Georgia’s Interests Section at the Swiss Embassy in Russia, and held it until December 2025, according to Kobakhidze. Kajaia succeeded Zurab Abashidze, who served as Special Representative from 2012 and was later appointed Kobakhidze’s advisor. articles.title: Kazakhstan considers new rules to flag risks in online games
articles.summary: The Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s parliament, has proposed a bill that would introduce labelling requirements for online games, allow them to be checked and potentially blocked if they pose a threat. Digital platforms would also be required to introduce parental controls so that children cannot access or download games without restrictions.
articles.body: The Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s parliament, has proposed a bill that would introduce labelling requirements for online games, allow them to be checked and potentially blocked if they pose a threat. Digital platforms would also be required to introduce parental controls so that children cannot access or download games without restrictions. Notably, the bill is being discussed just days before the release of «Grand Theft Auto 6.» The criteria outlined in the bill include in-game purchases and chat functions. These provisions could also cover popular multiplayer games such as «Counter-Strike 2» and «Dota 2.» The proposal was discussed during Government Hour on Nov. 16, while Deputy Chair of the Kurultai Dinara Zakiyeva introduced the initiative. «It is envisaged that the safety of all digital and information products, including online games, will be ensured by introducing requirements for platforms to label and describe their digital risks, such as the ability to chat and in-game purchases. Furthermore, the proposal provides for a mechanism for mandatory verification by an authorized government body, monitoring for violations, and requiring the removal or blocking of information or digital products if a threat or risk associated with such a product, such as a game, is identified,» Zakiyeva said. It has yet to be announced which government body will be responsible for checking the games, what fines platforms could face and what criteria will be used to assess risks. Platform owners will be held responsible for all identified violations. Meanwhile, players who preordered a digital copy of «Grand Theft Auto 6» could begin preloading the game on Nov. 10, while its official release is scheduled for Nov. 19. The bill is unlikely to be passed before then. Following the government’s conclusion, it will have to be reviewed by the Kurultai. It remains unclear how the regulations would apply to international digital stores and games that have already been released. The criteria outlined in the bill could also apply to other multiplayer games. «Counter-Strike 2» and «Dota 2» both feature in-game chat and purchases, exposing players to the risks that platforms would be required to flag. However, it remains unclear whether these provisions would cover such games or how they would apply to game developers and distribution platforms like Steam. Valve, the company behind both games and Steam, is also one of the largest foreign taxpayers in Kazakhstan .

articles.title: Kyrgyzstan to impose nationwide ban on plastic bags
articles.summary: Starting Jan. 1, 2027, the production, sale and free distribution of polyethylene bags will be prohibited in Kyrgyzstan, except for those that meet new requirements. President Sadyr Japarov said this during a meeting with residents of the Ton and Jeti-Oguz districts, Kaktus.media reported.
articles.body: Starting Jan. 1, 2027, the production, sale and free distribution of polyethylene bags will be prohibited in Kyrgyzstan, except for those that meet new requirements. President Sadyr Japarov said this during a meeting with residents of the Ton and Jeti-Oguz districts, Kaktus.media reported. Kyrgyzstan began restricting the use of polyethylene bags in 2023. At the time, the Issyk-Kul region restricted their sale to protect the resort area’s environment. However, local shops eventually returned to using plastic bags. An entrepreneur from the village of Bokonbaevo, who launched a paper bag production business two months ago, told Japarov about the development. «Everyone complied with the ban for the first and second years, but then, I don’t know, maybe people got distracted by the World Nomad Games or for some other reason, everyone switched to plastic bags,» the businessman said. Japarov responded that starting in January, the ban would apply nationwide. The president also pledged to meet with the entrepreneur in person and help him develop his business. Kyrgyzstan will also ban plastic coffee pods, egg packaging, plastic mesh packaging for food products and nonrecyclable single-use tableware. Meanwhile, plastic bottles and food containers will remain available for sale. In July 2025, they were removed from the list of prohibited items. Separately, Kazakhstan is also considering a ban on single-use tableware , including plastic cups, plates and cutlery, while helping develop an international agreement that would impose strict restrictions on such products, Vice Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Zhomart Aliyev said.

articles.body: Russia’s state corporation Rosatom is set to begin construction of Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant (NPP) on the shores of Lake Balkhash, near the village of Ulken in the Almaty region, in 2027, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy Almassadam Satkaliyev said. «As you know, during the state visit of Russian President Vladimir Putin to Kazakhstan this spring, Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev announced that construction could begin in 2027… If all the requirements under Kazakhstan’s legislation are met, we understand that Rosatom, together with Kazakhstani partners, namely Kazakhstani companies, could begin construction in 2027. This is the scenario we envisage,» he told reporters on the sidelines of World Atomic Days in Antalya, Turkey. According to him, cooperation between Rosatom, Kazakhstan Nuclear Power Plants (KNPP), the government and the Agency for Atomic Energy has been fairly successful over the past period. «We have already signed an intergovernmental agreement with Russia this year. An EPC contract has also been signed, and fairly constructive negotiations are currently underway on all the necessary annexes. Overall, this lays the groundwork for beginning construction of the nuclear power plant in the near future,» Satkaliyev said. He noted that Rosatom has unique experience in implementing international projects. According to Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev, the state corporation is currently involved in the construction of 28 reactors outside Russia. The first 2.4-gigawatt nuclear power plant is expected to cost $15 billion and is scheduled to be commissioned in 2035. China’s CNNC will build two nuclear power plants of similar capacity. The first of these will be located near the village of Ulken, close to Rosatom’s plant.

articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Azerbaijan is ready to further develop its partnership with NATO, based on mutual respect, shared interests and practical cooperation, Assistant to the President of Azerbaijan and Head of the Presidential Administration's Foreign Policy Affairs Department Hikmet Hajiyev said. According to the post on his X account, Hajiyev stated this during a meeting with NATO's Committee of Deputy Permanent Representatives in the “NATO+Azerbaijan” format. The meeting provided an opportunity to assess progress in Azerbaijan-NATO cooperation and discuss regional and international developments, he noted. Hajiyev emphasized Azerbaijan's contribution to international peace and security as a reliable NATO partner, including through its participation in international peace support operations. He added that cooperation between Azerbaijan and NATO had evolved over the years into a multifaceted partnership encompassing political dialogue and practical engagement in defence, security and capacity-building. "In 1994, Azerbaijan joined this partnership at a time of war and uncertainty. Today, we speak to you from a position of restored sovereignty, real peace and growing regional responsibility. Our partnership rests on mutual respect, shared interests and practical cooperation. We are ready to take it further, for a South Caucasus that is secure, connected and at peace," Hajiyev said.

articles.title: Albania Free Media Advocates Fear Anti-SLAPP Bill Isn’t Tough Enough
articles.summary: Media freedom groups in the country welcome draft legislation to protect journalists from abusive ‘SLAPP’ lawsuits – but want it to have more power to prevent legal assaults on freedom of speech.
articles.body: The government of Albania, an EU candidate state, last week put out a long-awaited draft law for publication introducing a new legal mechanism to protect journalists and media outlets from unfounded lawsuits or abusive court proceedings, known as SLAPPs. The draft legislation, part of Albania’s efforts to align domestic legislation with European law, aims to curb lawsuits that are often launched by wealthy and powerful people to put pressure on journalists and campaigners who speak out on matters of public interest. If it is adopted, the law will create procedural safeguards for people sued as a result of their engagement in matters of public interest. The key provisions will ensure that the legal costs of SLAPPs are borne by the claimants, the possible early dismissal of lawsuits deemed “manifestly unfounded”, priority handling of cases to prevent lengthy proceedings and give defendants the right to receive support from civil society organisations, unions or other entities.
