articles.title: AI and Uzbekistan’s Energy Sector: UN Urges Attention to Environmental Risks of Data Centers
articles.summary: The rapid development of artificial intelligence is driving up electricity and water consumption, placing additional pressure on energy infrastructure. This warning was issued on November 16 by Simon Stiell, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), during a high-level roundtable on green digital transformation at COP31 in Antalya.
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — The rapid development of artificial intelligence is driving up electricity and water consumption, placing additional pressure on energy infrastructure. This warning was issued on November 16 by Simon Stiell, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), during a high-level roundtable on green digital transformation at COP31 in Antalya. According to Stiell, artificial intelligence has enormous potential to address climate challenges, but its rapid expansion also brings significant environmental and economic risks. “Artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies are a double-edged sword. The challenge is to mitigate their harmful impacts, amplify their transformative potential, and use these technologies responsibly,” he emphasized. The Executive Secretary noted that growing electricity demand from data centers is placing additional strain on power systems. When this demand is met through fossil fuels, greenhouse gas emissions increase, making international climate goals more difficult to achieve. Another major concern is the transfer of energy infrastructure costs to consumers. According to Stiell, households and businesses should not have to face higher electricity bills, increased pollution contributing to global warming, and widening inequality in exchange for promises of future technological benefits. He also highlighted cases in which data center developers are building their own on-site gas-fired power plants to bypass existing grid constraints. Water consumption is another growing concern. In some countries, local communities are already opposing the construction of data centers due to concerns about water supplies, electricity costs, and environmental impacts. Against this backdrop, Stiell called on technology companies to disclose information about their energy and water consumption, improve infrastructure efficiency, and power data centers with renewable energy. “Claims of future emissions savings cannot justify increasing pollution today,” he stated. At the same time, the head of the UN climate secretariat stressed that artificial intelligence could become an important tool for climate change adaptation. In particular, AI technologies can improve early warning systems for floods, help farmers prepare for droughts, increase the efficiency of electricity grids, and facilitate the integration of solar and wind power generation. Stiell also emphasized the need to ensure that developing countries have access to financing, computing capacity, and reliable data. According to him, the energy transition risks progressing at different speeds in developed and developing economies. Artificial intelligence should help bridge this gap rather than widen it. For Uzbekistan, which is expanding its digital infrastructure and renewable energy capacity, these issues are of practical importance. The growth of computing capacity requires careful consideration of electricity availability, grid resilience, and efficient water resource management. COP31 also saw the introduction of the Antalya AI Pledge, a voluntary framework aimed at reducing the environmental impact of artificial intelligence and promoting AI-powered climate solutions.

articles.title: Kazakh central bank plans 30% private pension asset transfer
articles.summary: By 2030, private investment portfolio managers (IPMs) in Kazakhstan could oversee 20% to 30% of the country’s pension assets, the Qazaq Association of Minority Shareholders (QAMS) reported, citing Kazakhstan’s Capital Market Development Program for 2026-2030. The plan covers not only the savings of contributors who have chosen to transfer their funds from the National Bank ...
articles.body: By 2030, private investment portfolio managers (IPMs) in Kazakhstan could oversee 20% to 30% of the country’s pension assets, the Qazaq Association of Minority Shareholders (QAMS) reported , citing Kazakhstan’s Capital Market Development Program for 2026-2030. The plan covers not only the savings of contributors who have chosen to transfer their funds from the National Bank of Kazakhstan to private managers, but also a portion of the pension assets currently managed by the National Bank. Under the proposed arrangement, the bank would delegate some of these assets to private IPMs under specific investment mandates. Under the proposed model, private managers would be selected through a competitive bidding process to oversee a portion of pension assets. During the initial phase, the National Bank would retain responsibility for setting investment policy and overseeing risk management. Plans for 2027 include developing standardized criteria for selecting managers, defining investment mandates and benchmarks, and establishing a framework for working with multiple managers. The arrangement is scheduled to be tested in a regulatory sandbox in 2027-2028. In the following years, the volume of assets transferred, the number of participating managers and the range of investment strategies are expected to increase gradually. Initially, private firms could be entrusted with portfolios of government securities. The range of eligible assets is expected to expand over time to include corporate bonds, shares in Kazakhstani companies and other asset classes. Managers’ performance would be assessed against benchmarks, as well as on their compliance with investment mandates and established risk limits. If a firm underperforms, the volume of assets entrusted to it could be reduced or transferred to another manager. According to the Unified Accumulative Pension Fund (UAPF), as of Oct. 1, 2026, the National Bank managed 26.63 trillion tenge (approximately $60 billion) in pension assets, accounting for 99.24% of the fund’s total assets of 26.84 trillion tenge. Private firms, by comparison, managed just over 206 billion tenge ($460 million), or 0.76% of the total. If private managers take on 20% to 30% of pension assets by 2030, their combined portfolios would amount to approximately 5.37 trillion to 8.05 trillion tenge. That would be 26 to 39 times the current volume of assets under their management. Achieving this target would therefore require private IPMs to expand their portfolios substantially over the next few years. However, the figures reflect a proposed model, and the actual volume of assets transferred will depend on the criteria for selecting managers and how the program is implemented.

articles.title: Azerbaijan, Georgia seek faster rail freight movement across border
articles.summary: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Azerbaijan Railways CJSC (ADY) and Georgian Railways management have discussed the acceleration of the border crossing by freight trains.
articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Azerbaijan Railways CJSC (ADY) and Georgian Railways management have discussed the acceleration of the border crossing by freight trains. The discussion took place during the visit of a delegation led by the Chairman of ADY, Rovshan Rustamov, to the Boyuk Kasik, Gardabani, and Tbilisi railway stations, the ADY reported. During the visit, discussions included the expansion of cooperation to ensure more efficient organization of rail transport between the two countries and to accelerate border-crossing processes. The processes for receiving, processing, and dispatching trains at stations, as well as the capabilities of the existing infrastructure, were reviewed. The primary focus was on reducing the transit time for freight and passenger trains at the Azerbaijan–Georgia border, optimizing border and customs control procedures, ensuring the uninterrupted movement of trains, and eliminating potential delays. The delegation also reviewed the work being carried out at the Gardabani and Tbilisi stations regarding the organization of transport, the coordination of train movements, and the improvement of operational processes. The parties emphasized the importance of refining operational mechanisms, simplifying technical procedures, eliminating redundant operations, and facilitating the prompt exchange of information. The status of the implementation of previous agreements was also reviewed during the meeting. It has been reported that positive results have been achieved in organizing the uninterrupted movement of trains along the Boyuk Kasik–Tbilisi–Boyuk Kasik route and in optimizing technical inspection procedures for railcars. According to ADY , new operational approaches implemented within the framework of previous agreements have made it possible to halve the time required for freight trains to cross the border. During the meeting, it was noted that these measures serve to strengthen railway ties between the two countries, enhance the efficiency of international freight transport, reduce transit times, and boost the competitiveness of the Middle Corridor.

articles.title: Tajikistan's installed power generation capacity exceeds 6,700 MW
articles.summary: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Tajikistan’s installed power generation capacity has exceeded 6,700 megawatts (MW), following the construction of new generating facilities and the modernization of existing power plants.
articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Tajikistan’s installed power generation capacity has exceeded 6,700 megawatts (MW), following the construction of new generating facilities and the modernization of existing power plants. According to Tajikistan’s Ministry of Energy and Water Resources, Minister Daler Juma announced this on November 12 during an address to the Majlisi Namoyandagon, the lower chamber of the Majlisi Oli (Supreme Assembly) of Tajikistan. He provided an overview of the current state of the country’s energy sector, its performance, and development prospects. Since gaining independence, Tajikistan has implemented 37 state investment projects in the energy sector, with a combined value of 30 billion somoni (approximately $3.25 billion). Another 20 projects, worth 23 billion somoni (approximately $2.49 billion), are currently underway. The commissioning of more than 2,300 MW of new generating capacity has brought the country's total installed capacity to over 6,700 MW. Electricity production has also increased, from 17.4 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 1991 to 24 billion kWh in 2025. The rehabilitation and modernization of existing hydropower plants (HPPs) remain among the sector's key priorities. Following the rehabilitation of three generating units at the Nurek HPP, its installed capacity increased by 120 MW. The plant's modernization is scheduled for completion in 2031, when its total capacity is expected to reach 3,375 MW. The rehabilitation of the Qayroqqum, Sarband, and Varzob-1 HPPs has also increased their generating capacity.

articles.title: IMF backs further increases in Uzbekistan energy tariffs
articles.summary: The IMF supports further utility and energy tariff increases in Uzbekistan to bring prices closer to cost-recovery levels, with compensation for vulnerable groups.
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — The International Monetary Fund (IMF) supports further increases in utility and energy tariffs in Uzbekistan to gradually bring them to cost-recovery levels. Prices for liquefied gas are also set to rise from 15 November, with compensation planned for vulnerable groups, IMF Resident Representative Koba Gvenetadze said. He made the remarks at a presentation of the regional economic outlook at the Central Bank of Uzbekistan. According to Gvenetadze, tariff reform has been one of the factors slowing the decline in inflation towards the Central Bank's target. Utility price increases initially affected businesses before being extended to households. The IMF supported the process because keeping tariffs low would encourage excessive energy consumption and increase the burden of energy subsidies on the state budget. "We fully supported it because it was absolutely necessary. Otherwise, it would have encouraged excessive energy consumption in Uzbekistan while also creating a large bill for energy subsidies in the budget," Gvenetadze said. However, current tariffs still do not cover the costs of providing utility services and energy resources. In the IMF representative's assessment, prices should gradually move towards cost-recovery levels. This would help the Central Bank make progress towards its inflation target. Gvenetadze also announced an upcoming increase in liquefied gas prices. "Starting from 15 November, there will also be an increase in liquefied gas prices. However, the necessary funds will be allocated to vulnerable groups that may be affected by this increase," he added. Central Bank Deputy Chairman Nodirbek Achilov also called for state support to be targeted. He stressed that subsidies fall under fiscal and structural policy rather than the Central Bank's monetary policy instruments. According to Achilov, subsidies provided by the Ministry of Economy and Finance or the Energy Ministry should have clearly defined recipient groups and limited durations. "If the Ministry of Economy and Finance or the Energy Ministry wants to provide a subsidy, it should be well targeted and time-limited. It should include an expiry clause specifying when the subsidy will end," Achilov said. The Central Bank cannot prevent the direct impact of tariff increases on prices. However, the regulator monitors their secondary effects on inflation expectations, wages and the prices of other goods and services. Achilov said the Central Bank was keeping its policy rate sufficiently high to contain these effects and prevent a persistent inflationary spiral. A study included in the IMF's inflation report examines the relationship between fuel subsidies and the effects of supply shocks. According to the study's findings, in countries with high levels of fuel subsidies, the impact of such shocks on inflation is around half as strong. However, their primary budget balance deteriorates significantly three years after the shock. This means that subsidies can reduce short-term inflationary pressure by limiting price increases, but may also increase the burden on public finances.

articles.title: Kallas: EU views South Caucasus as part of strategy to diversify ties – Exclusive
articles.summary: The EU views the development of alternative transport, energy, and digital routes through the South Caucasus and Central Asia as an important part of efforts to diversify ties between Europe and Asia amid the blockage of major maritime routes, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told Report while commenting on today's ministerial meeting on security and connectivity."We see the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz,…
articles.body: The EU views the development of alternative transport, energy, and digital routes through the South Caucasus and Central Asia as an important part of efforts to diversify ties between Europe and Asia amid the blockage of major maritime routes, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told Report while commenting on today's ministerial meeting on security and connectivity."We see the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which means that - and also the blockade of the Black Sea corridor, now also Bab-el-Mandeb - which means that all the countries are looking for trade corridors that are alternatives to those that already exist. And there, I mean, connecting Asia with Europe, there the Central Asia, South Caucasus, and Black Sea countries are really of great importance. We are discussing energy connectivity also to have alternatives for energy. We are discussing, you know, the digital connectivity because everything is dependent on the digital connections at the moment. We really feel that this is mutual for the partners of the region, as well as for us to have alternatives and develop this further," the EU foreign policy chief noted.She emphasized that the diversification of ties meets the mutual interests of the European Union and its partners.When asked about the role of security issues on the meeting's agenda, Kallas confirmed that this topic also holds a central place in the discussions."It's also a security issue, absolutely. I mean, we have seen that every connection that you have, the other side might also hurt you. So you need to diversify your connections. That is the aim," she said.The ministerial meeting on cross-regional security and connectivity is taking place today in Brussels following the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting, with the participation of representatives from the South Caucasus, Central Asia, Moldova, Türkiye, and Ukraine.This is already the second meeting in this format involving the foreign ministers of EU member states and partners from the South Caucasus, Central Asia, Moldova, Türkiye, and Ukraine.The discussions focus on the development of transport, energy, and digital links, as well as issues of regional security.

articles.title: IMF urges Uzbekistan to assess budget without gold revenue
articles.summary: The IMF has urged Uzbekistan to assess its budget balance excluding gold revenue and limit spending increases when revenues exceed targets.
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has recommended that Uzbekistan assess its budget balance excluding gold revenue. The authorities have responded openly to the proposal, IMF Resident Representative Koba Gvenetadze said. He presented the recommendation at a regional economic outlook presentation at the Central Bank of Uzbekistan. Uzbekistan's state budget deficit stood at 2.1% of GDP in 2025, below the target of 3%. The same target has been set for 2026. Gold revenue remains one of the factors affecting budget income. Uzbekistan is among the world's largest gold producers, and prices for the metal remain high. Gvenetadze warned that rising gold revenue could encourage the government to increase public spending. "There may be a temptation, which can be explained from a political economy perspective, to pursue pro-cyclical policies and increase spending. But at the same time, these revenues need to be saved," he said. The fund discussed with the Uzbek authorities the possibility of switching to an analysis of the non-mineral budget balance. This indicator makes it possible to assess the state of public finances without revenue from natural resource extraction. Oil-exporting countries use a non-oil balance for similar purposes. In Uzbekistan's case, the proposal is to exclude gold revenue from the calculations. "If you have one commodity that generates a large share of your revenue, this indicator allows you to see what is happening to the budget deficit without it. In Uzbekistan's case, that commodity is gold. The Uzbek authorities were very open to this idea," Gvenetadze said. Other IMF recommendations include limiting spending increases when revenues exceed planned levels. The fund also called for avoiding untargeted subsidies and reducing tax incentives. "It is important to avoid tax holidays because, once introduced, they are difficult to get rid of," the IMF representative said. He said businesses place greater importance on sustainable economic development and predictable tax policy. Gvenetadze described the current period as a suitable time to implement reforms. He used the metaphor: "You should repair the roof while the sun is shining." The IMF representative added that public debt remained low and fiscal sustainability was not under pressure. Ulmas Juraev, head of a department within the Ministry of Economy and Finance's tax and customs policy department, outlined measures to improve fiscal transparency. He said that, following an IMF mission to assess compliance with the Fiscal Transparency Code, the ministry had published a report on tax expenditures for the first time. It had also presented a methodology for assessing them. Both documents have been published on the Open Budget portal. Juraev added that the moratorium on tax inspections could result in lost budget revenue. In response, the ministry plans to discuss with the IMF how to modernise the audit system, taking into account the moratorium's three-year duration.

articles.title: Uzbekistan nears completion of bridge over Ferghana Canal
articles.summary: A 15-metre-wide bridge over the Ferghana Canal in Namangan region is nearing completion, alongside road repairs on the route to the Kyrgyz border.
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan is nearing completion of the reconstruction of a bridge over the Ferghana Canal in Uchkurghan district, Namangan region, on the D 128 highway leading to the Kyrgyz border. The updated bridge is expected to open in the coming days. The work is being carried out on the D 128 state highway, known as the Uchkurghan–Boston–Kyrgyz Republic border road. The route provides access to the Uchkurghan–Kengsay customs post. The new bridge is being built to replace the previous 9-metre-wide structure and will be 15 metres wide. This will expand the capacity for vehicle traffic. Asphalt paving on the bridge has been completed. The structure is now being prepared for commissioning. Repairs and widening of the road along the same route are also nearing completion. The work is being carried out by the state institution responsible for road maintenance in Uchkurghan district. The road works are expected to be fully completed in the coming days. The upgraded road will then also be opened to traffic. The bridge reconstruction and road repairs are intended to improve transport links in the border area. The upgraded infrastructure is expected to provide additional convenience for passenger and freight transport.

articles.title: EU loses diplomatic advantages, lacks position for talks with Russia — expert
articles.summary: According to Andrea Bianchi, the premise that the EU’s ruling class "cannot afford to lose the political capital invested" in the Ukraine project since 2022 has limited its room for maneuver
articles.body: BRUSSELS, November 16. /TASS/. The European Union has failed to appoint a negotiator and formulate a position for dialogue with Russia, as the bloc is no longer capable of conducting diplomacy or navigating geography and history, Andrea Bianchi, an Italian expert who collaborates with Russia’s Valdai International Discussion Club, told TASS. "From what I see in Brussels and hear in Italy, there is no bilaterally acceptable negotiator in Europe. Today, the EU’s political class lacks a grasp of history. Geography is deliberately forgotten. Diplomacy is mostly practiced in `transparent’ ways. In this way Europe loses all the benefits of covert, cultural, long-term, disciplined diplomatic exchange and mutual understanding of the guarantees and requests of the other side," the expert argued, commenting on the results of the Abu Dhabi talks on Ukraine and two European summits in Dublin. "The EU does not have a mandate for negotiation either. While a national foreign ministry speaks for a state whose government can take decisions and be held to account for them, the EEAS (European External Action Service - TASS) stands for 27 governments that often disagree on basic questions due to geography and culture," he explained. "The EEAS can speak clearly only when all 27 states agree, and when they do not, its 'diplomacy' shrinks to carefully balanced communiques. On Washington, Russia, Ukraine and the Middle East, the result has been the lowest common denominator dressed up as strategy," Bianchi emphasized. According to him, the premise that the EU’s ruling class "cannot afford to lose the political capital invested" in the Ukraine project since 2022 has limited its room for maneuver. Moreover, non-EU member Britain undermining all processes related to the Ukraine talks "literally destroys any chance for the EU’s ruling class to even approach the diplomatic talks in a constructive way," the expert concluded. At the November 13 summit in Dublin, the EU leaders only managed to agree on a negotiating team that will be the same one that travelled to Abu Dhabi to support Kiev last week. Namely, the EU’s executive and decision-making arms, the European Commission (EC) and the European Council, respectively, along with five countries - Germany, France, Italy, Poland and non-EU member United Kingdom - will spearhead Ukraine talks. Following the summit, EC President Ursula von der Leyen pledged that EU foreign ministers would adopt additional sanctions on Russia as early as November 16, during a meeting in Brussels. The EU is set to contribute to the negotiations through pressure on Moscow, she insisted.

articles.title: Coles investigates cyber-attack and apologises to customers
articles.summary: Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data compromised but recommends updating passwords as a precaution Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised.
articles.body: Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised. Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. “Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange. “We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems. “Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.” Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”. “We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said. “We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.” Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they received unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links. In a separate and unrelated incident, Woolworths said it was aware of reports from customers who purchased compromised e-gift cards. The ABC first reported on Monday some customers had lost hundreds of dollars after buying the company’s Everyday WISH gift cards through its rewards website or app, only to find the sums loaded on to them had been spent by someone else. Some customers told the national broadcaster they had lost up to $500, with transactions showing up at stores in different states to where they purchased the cards. “We are aware of reports of an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and are looking into the matter as a priority,” a Woolworths spokesperson said in a statement. “We recognise the concern this has caused affected customers and we apologise to customers impacted. We encourage any customer who notices a transaction they don’t recognise to contact our Gift Card Support team.” The company says it is working through all reported issues and will look into replacing affected e-gift cards.

articles.title: Iran says it targeted US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary: First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months.
articles.body: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months. “This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.” US Central Command denied that the radar system had been destroyed and said US forces had intercepted two Iranian drones headed for Bahrain . Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes. Trump said he had asked the vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states. Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal. Vance has been at the forefront of Republicans saying the war was the cause of the widespread Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public because higher diesel prices were a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. An opinion poll in the UK showed 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu). It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was 45%, with 22% opposed. The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda. Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.” Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon. In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for a review of Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”. The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning. Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely in political and security circles. Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested. The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

articles.title: Color revolutions now built into Western playbook — Russian MFA
articles.summary: The role of information and education as instruments for undermining sovereignty has grown sharply, Russian State Secretary and Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Yevgeny Ivanov noted
articles.body: MOSCOW, November 16. /TASS/. It's now "common practice" for the West to organize color revolutions and interfere in elections in countries of the world majority, Russian State Secretary and Deputy Foreign Minister Yevgeny Ivanov said. "Today, Western countries are clinging to the remnants of their former dominance. They are trying to hold back the development of countries of the world majority and preserve a system of unequal economic relations by every means available. They continue to make extensive use of neocolonial tools. The role of information and education as instruments for undermining sovereignty has grown sharply. Interference in elections and other domestic political processes, including the organization of color revolutions, has become common practice," Ivanov said at the General Assembly of the Forum of Supporters of the Struggle against Modern Practices of Neocolonialism, "For the Freedom of Nations!".

articles.title: Burnham sets three tests for EU deal, saying it should make Brexit ‘closer to what people thought they were voting for’ – UK politics live
articles.summary: PM to address fallout from Brexit in speech this evening Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ Following the Russell Brand conviction, and the revelations about David Walliams, there have been calls for the government to introduce a “staggered” age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds.
articles.body: When Andy Burnham told the Labour conference that he wanted to start a debate on a new relationship with the EU, because Brexit had done more harm than good, he raised the possibility that this could lead to Labour proposing to rejoin at some point after the next election. But some ministers and Labour MPs are deeply unhappy about that prospect, believing that there would have to be a referendum and that this would be deeply divisive, and there are some signs that Burnham (who is on record as saying he would like the UK to rejoin in his lifetime) is starting to scale back his ambitions. In his speech to the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham repeated the argument he made in September about Brexit having done more harm than good. But he focused on making Brexit better, not overturning it. At one point in the speech he said: double quotation mark I don’t believe Brexit and the deal that they got has been good enough for Britain. I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years. And actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016. double quotation mark People’s jobs depend on working together and collaborating. And that’s our approach, and it will always be our approach. People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are. And yes, working with the European Union, as I said, but at the same time, respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result. The reference to “respecting the referendum result” could have just meant not rejoining before the next election. But given that this was a manifesto red line, and that he had already spoken about respecting that, he seemed to imply something more. And today Burnham has announced three tests for his Brexit reset. (See 9.15am .) Although these are only tests for the deal he is announcing on Friday, not for the Brexit policy he will announce at the next election, the focus on improving the Brexit deal and bringing it “closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016” might be a sign of where his thinking is heading. In interviews this morning, Ed Miliband , the foreign secretary, also focused on the government wanting to make Brexit work better for the economy. He told Sky News: double quotation mark Look, here’s my starting point. My constituents, people across the country, voted for a range of reasons for Brexit, but one of them was one of the biggest, certainly for my constituents, was to make our economy better, positive economic change. We haven’t had that. The economy has got worse. And nobody really thinks this Brexit deal is a good deal. On ITV’s Good Morning Britain, Ed Balls did not ask Miliband about Russell Brand but he did ask him repeatedly if he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU. (See 9.15am .) Miliband and Balls worked very closely together for many years and Balls was clearly assuming that the honest answer would be “Yes”. But Miliband said that he would not give his own personal view because he was abiding by collective cabinet responsibility. Balls said that Andy Burnham has been happy to say he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime, while John Healey (who is 10 years older) has said that he does not expect that in his lifetime. Balls asked Miliband what he expected to happen in his lifetime. Miliband still refused to answer. Balls urged him to be braver and less restrained – “Let your hair down, have a good time” - but Miliband still would not engage with the question.

articles.title: Closure of border with Russia to deal blow to businesses in Narva — city officials
articles.summary: Narva City Council Chair Urbo Vaarmann said that the city authorities expect the government to provide financially backed assistance to affected companies, support in creating new jobs and attracting investment and long-term solutions to residents’ utility issues
articles.body: VILNIUS, November 16. /TASS/. The potential closure of the Estonian-Russian border could seriously impact businesses in Narva and jeopardize jobs, Narva City Council Chair Urbo Vaarmann stated. "Therefore, we expect the government to provide specific, financially backed assistance to affected companies, support in creating new jobs and attracting investment, and long-term solutions to residents’ utility issues. These steps must be coordinated with the city and business owners before any potential restrictions [on the border with Russia] take effect," the Postimees newspaper quoted the official as saying. On November 15, Estonian Interior Minister Igor Taro said that a decision to close the border with Russia would be made at a cabinet meeting, and that the measures could be temporary or permanent. Meanwhile, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna clarified that Tallinn would close all border crossings on the Estonian-Russian border starting December 1. Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova previously told TASS that Moscow would verify information about Estonia's intention to close all border crossings. If true, she emphasized, it would be yet another "outburst of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia.".

articles.title: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
articles.summary: Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.
articles.body: Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency. The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand , push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence. He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025. White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained. The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal , which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec. The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject ; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers. Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency. Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”. Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west. Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine , which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms. However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms. That is believed to be unpalatable to China , which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia. Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful. Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said. Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US. “Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum . “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.” Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate. “The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.” With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

articles.title: Estonia prepares cloud-based digital government to keep public services running in case of occupation
articles.summary: Estonia is developing technological infrastructure that will allow the government to keep digital public services running even if the country is occupied or its data centres are destroyed. To this end, the authorities are creating secure cloud systems that will operate outside the country.
articles.body: Estonia is developing technological infrastructure that will allow the government to keep digital public services running even if the country is occupied or its data centres are destroyed. To this end, the authorities are creating secure cloud systems that will operate outside the country. Source: Politico Details: Estonia plans to use Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and its own government platform. The country is developing secure systems capable of operating beyond its borders, including at a dedicated government data repository in Luxembourg and other locations across Europe. This will allow public services to continue operating even if the country's domestic digital infrastructure is destroyed or damaged during a war. Estonia already stores backup copies of government data in Luxembourg, including information from population and land registers, as well as copies of legislation. The country now wants to ensure that these data can not only be stored abroad but also be used to keep government institutions fully operational during a war or another major crisis. "Now we want to stay online under any circumstances. All critical services must remain operational," explained Tõnis Grünberg, one of the architects of the strategy and a former official at Estonia's Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs. One of the factors that prompted this approach was Estonia's experience of cyberattacks in 2007. At the time, the country faced 22 days of large-scale attacks that disrupted numerous government and commercial services. The Estonian authorities subsequently blamed Russia for the attacks. Estonia then significantly upgraded its digital infrastructure and became one of the most digitally advanced countries in the world. Estonia is now preparing for more serious threats, including the physical destruction of data centres or the occupation of its territory. According to Allan Allmere, an adviser at the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, the aim is not merely to preserve government information but also to ensure that the government can continue using it during a crisis. Other countries are gradually taking an interest in a similar approach. For example, the United Kingdom and Norway are exploring the possibility of establishing their own "digital embassies", where they would securely store each other's data. This model would allow countries to reduce their dependence on physical infrastructure within their own borders and spread risks across several countries. Meanwhile, Estonia plans to ensure the long-term accessibility of information so that government data remain understandable and usable even decades into the future. articles.title: Barristers could be barred from practice over use of rape myths, warns justice secretary
articles.summary: Move follows Russell Brand trial, in which his barrister argued comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not ‘resisted’ UK politics live – latest updates Barristers could be barred from practice if they perpetuate rape myths to defend clients, the justice secretary has said after Russell Brand’s trial.
articles.body: Barristers could be barred from practice if they perpetuate rape myths to defend clients, the justice secretary has said after Russell Brand’s trial. Alex Norris has written to the body that regulates barristers amid concern over the tactics deployed by the comedian’s counsel. In his letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Norris said it was “unacceptable” for the profession to “perpetuate myths” about rape victims in court, and warned that those who broke the rules could face disciplinary action. A series of rape myths were allegedly deployed in the defence of Brand, 51, during his trial at Southwark crown court, including the argument that his accusers should not be believed because they had not screamed, kicked or fled. Brand was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults. In his closing speech to the jury, Brand’s defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, argued that the comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”. Winter asked the jury whether they could be sure that of the “many, many women” Brand had slept with over a decade, he had “raped just three of them”. Winter has reported himself to the BSB after criticisms over an exchange with a Sunday Times journalist outside court as well as his conduct within it. Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: “[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large.” A spokesperson for the BSB told the Times it agreed that rape and sexual assault cases “must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice”. They added: “That is one of the reasons why we set up an expert reference group to advise on strengthening standards for barristers acting in rape and serious sexual offence cases.” A spokesperson for the Bar Council, which represents barristers, told the paper that a defendant denying a rape charge had a right to have evidence tested in court, and stressed the importance of the BSB remaining independent of the government. In a separate development, Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, shared a message from her jailed husband in which he claimed he was “not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening”. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said Brand’s message was “disgusting” and apologised for appearing on the disgraced comedian’s online show as Labour leader in 2015. Miliband told Sky News: “His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it’s revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments. “I’ve said that if I’d known any of these allegations against him, I would never have done that interview, and I regret doing it.” Meanwhile, the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, urged the entertainment industry to “get its house in order” or face a government crackdown. She is due to meet senior media, arts and sports figures on Monday and will call on them to introduce systems to protect young employees and freelancers from harassment and abuse by older, more powerful men. Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from the category B Wandsworth prison in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.

articles.title: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
articles.summary: Prime minister promises ‘root-and-branch rethink’ of support for young people as Milburn report advises sweeping changes to some benefits Andy Burnham: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood…
articles.body: Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”. Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools. Writing in the Guardian, the prime minister said ministers’ response to Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into the crisis of youth unemployment in the UK would not be “a traditional … reform” but “societal and generational”. He promised to reduce the number of Neets – 18- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – which topped a million this year for the first time in more than a decade. Hoping to head off opposition from leftwing MPs in his own party, who rebelled to block Starmer’s welfare changes last summer , Burnham said the government would “invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on”, but said the support “will have to come with responsibilities”. “If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can. Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” said Burnham. Milburn’s long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s . Some young people will lose their personal independence payments and the right to claim the health element of universal credit, and instead will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit. The report will also recommend cutting national insurance payments by businesses for employees aged between 21 and 24 for a five-year period, starting in retail and hospitality. The move could cost as much as £5bn, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank. The government has also announced it will expand a taxpayer-funded scheme aimed at helping young people into work to under-25s who have been claiming benefits for a year. Eligible 18- to 24-year-olds will be “guaranteed” a fully funded, six-month job matched to their skills after 12 months on universal credit. The Liberal Democrats said the six-month offering was worth “very little” without a job at the end of it. Before the publication of the report, Milburn said the government would have to be “candid with people”, that it would take 10 years for the benefits bill to come down, and investment would have to be made upfront. Addressing critics calling for the benefits bill to be immediately slashed, the former health secretary told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “There’s no such thing as a free lunch. If you are going to will the ends, you’ve got to will the means. I don’t think there’s a single person in this country who believes that it’s tolerable to have one million young people, aged 16 to 24, who are not in education, employment, or training.” Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, acknowledged that Milburn’s review would have an “element of compulsion” for Neets and there would be people who would receive less in benefits than currently. He said the UK had to become more like countries that had dealt with youth unemployment more successfully, such as the Netherlands, where the youth desk would “literally knock on your door” and offer options of training or work. But he denied that Milburn was proposing a ban on young people claiming health-related benefits. “That’s not what he’s saying. He’s saying if you have a long-term disability, that means you can never work,” he said. “You will actually get more than you will now. He’s saying that if you have extra costs, there will be a benefit you can apply to for extra costs. He’s also saying there should be a local fund for short-term needs, and for other people, he’s saying there should be more support to get into work. Change was necessary, he added, because the number of young people claiming personal independence payments (Pip) had doubled since the start of the decade, while the number of young people on the health element of universal credit had increased by 80%. Burnham hit out at the Conservatives and Reform, who have called for deep and immediate cuts to welfare, with Kemi Badenoch vowing to slash the bill by £36.1bn by 2030 if the party wins the next general election. Under the plans 70% of child benefit disability-related claims linked to ADHD and “milder” behavioural disorders and learning disabilities would be cut, with Labour calling the proposals “ a charter for human misery ”. The shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, acknowledged the plans could mean around half a million children losing disability-related payments. “This is to help those children,” she told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg, adding that under the plans, child mental health services would receive £1bn of funding. “The point of that funding is because there are children who are struggling. Let’s use this funding in the best possible way to support those children.” Burnham accused past Conservative governments of taking “a deliberate decision to make young people bear the brunt” of austerity cuts. “What is the Tory solution now? To punish those young people once again,” he said. “The crude cuts they are proposing … would simply compound the mistakes they made in government. They would drive children into poverty and increase levels of family homelessness even further, piling further pressure on councils, the NHS and other public services. This is not “reform”. It is a path to higher public spending and broken services.” A survey of young people by the Children’s Commissioner, which received more than 1m responses, found that more than half said they were worried about getting a good john in the future. The responses revealed that the UK’s young people want to work but face “huge challenges” finding experience and opportunities, said Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England. “The message is clear. Young people are ambitious, they want to work, they want a good job,” she said. “We need to help them get the skills, the experience and opportunities to find work. “They need a full, rich education that gives them the knowledge and skills to get on in life, but too many are being let down by the advice and careers support they receive, which many young people do not feel isn’t good enough.” Responding to the survey, Milburn said he had not met a single young person who wanted to be Neet while writing the review. “All too often the system – from health to welfare to the labour market – has failed them. That’s why a fundamental system reset is needed to give hope back to young people,” he said.

articles.title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
articles.summary: PM to meet European leaders at summit this week aiming to secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’ Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.
articles.body: Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU. It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU. Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential. “It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.” It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016. And it passes the so-called “ Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives. “This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.” However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies. He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement. The exit clause, previously nicknamed the “Farage clause” , is designed to guard against any the cost of potentially reversing any reset on Friday should the UK’s political landscape change. The cost of infrastructure at the borders has largely been paid for by private companies, including Eurotunnel, but French staff the food checks there, at Calais port and at Boulogne-sur-Mer, where all fish checks take place. Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue. He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority. He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

articles.title: What to expect from Trump and Xi's upcoming meeting in China
articles.summary: Preview of what to expect as President Trump meets with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China this week.
articles.body: Preview of what to expect as President Trump meets with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China this week. ROB SCHMITZ, HOST: President Trump will meet with some of the world's most powerful leaders this week. China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin and President Trump will be among the attendees to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen China. But while the administration says nuclear proliferation is on the docket, all eyes will be on the U.S.-China relationship. That's now under serious strain after the scandalous departure of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, following revelations regarding a romantic relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Evan Osnos writes for The New Yorker. He has covered China for much of his career and is closely following the APEC summit. Welcome. EVAN OSNOS: Thanks, Rob. SCHMITZ: So let's start with what's been dominating headlines this week, NVIDIA. You know, this scandal is hanging over this upcoming meeting between Trump and Xi Jinping. How do you think this will set the tone? OSNOS: Well, it is a huge development to happen right before a meeting at this altitude of two leaders. I mean, you have now a case that has brought the underlying issues right to the surface, and by that I mean the tension around technology and chips and more specifically, what the Trump administration has set out to do when it comes to allowing or restricting the export of American chips and who it's been listening to. So, you know, Jensen Huang has been one of the president's most trusted voices over the course of the last two years of this administration on technology issues. He is now gone, and so they go into this summit with a scrambled set of inputs. And it's not entirely clear how that's going to play out in the room. SCHMITZ: So I want to pivot to another trade issue here. This week, China extended its trade truce over rare earth exports by two more months to January 10, and for its part, the U.S. is extending tariff exclusions on 178 Chinese products until that date. What is at stake here if these two sides cannot come to an agreement? OSNOS: Well, it's an explosive prospect. But they have managed to avoid having these full tariffs go into effect now for many months, and that's by mutual design. I mean, the - China's economy has weakness on the domestic side. They're still dealing with the outcome of a property collapse, which left 90 million houses unfilled - enough people, by the way, to house the entire population of Russia. They've had youth unemployment - at some points, up above 20%. So they were not eager to get into a trade war. And of course, on the United States' side, Donald Trump's party was just battered in the midterms partly because of the effects of tariffs introduced into trade relationships around the world. So in some ways, he's had reasons to try to hold this off. If, in fact, the truce collapses and they're not able to figure out a way to push this off, this could trigger another round of retaliatory tariffs and a spiral of retaliation that could drive up prices for American consumers. And that comes, obviously, at a moment when voters have signaled pretty loudly that they don't want to see that happen. So the stakes are high for the administration on that score. SCHMITZ: You mentioned the midterms. President Trump took, obviously, a major loss during these midterms, and come January, he's going to be facing a Democrat-controlled Congress. He's only got two years left as president. Is Xi Jinping looking beyond President Trump at this stage? OSNOS: He doesn't have the luxury of being able to write Trump off, but he certainly does come into this meeting knowing that Trump doesn't have a tailwind. Politically, he doesn't have the kind of support in Washington that he could count on if he wanted to try to restart this tariff war. It is, in any diplomatic encounter, sort of job No. 1 - is to understand what your counterpart's vulnerabilities are. That is the thing that you're always asking your intelligence services to give you a briefing on beforehand. And in this case, Xi Jinping comes in with a knowledge of Trump's significant vulnerabilities. But he also knows, and I think this is really important to remember, that from the first term, he got a pretty clear indication that Trump can turn on a dime. And in the latter years of Trump's first administration, when he started to struggle after the midterms and the COVID pandemic came in and began to drag down the economy, he turned his sights on China, started blaming it for the COVID pandemic. He blamed it for his struggles in the 2020 election, and China found itself suddenly in the crosshairs. So I think the Xi Jinping cohort in the Chinese leadership has that memory, and they know that he is somebody you can't quite write off. SCHMITZ: That is Evan Osnos. He's a staff writer for The New Yorker. Evan, thank you. OSNOS: My pleasure. Thanks, Rob. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved.
